coffee.headline: 634 reviews, averaging 4.20★. Taste carries the category — and the complaint vocabulary says exactly what goes wrong with it: the word that most distinguishes a low-rated coffee review from a high-rated one is “weak”.
coffee.fix_argument: Taste complaints appear in 25% of coffee reviews and account for an estimated 0.16★ of drag on the category average — more than the next four fixable themes combined. The costliest single complaint is a different one: when a coffee arrives stale or unlike its description, that review runs 0.84★ lower, but it only happens in 6% of reviews, so it contributes 0.05★ overall. Fix taste consistency for reach; fix condition for severity.
coffee.language_argument: Praise runs on “morning”, “rich” and “blend” — ritual and body. Complaint runs on “weak”, “description” and “machine”. Both complaint terms point the same way: the coffee under-delivered against what the listing promised, rather than being bad in the abstract. Lead with strength and brew guidance, not with adjectives.

snack.headline: 558 reviews at 4.34★ — a well-liked category where the complaints are unusually specific: “sea salt” and “oil” are among the strongest markers of a low-rated review.
snack.fix_argument: Taste complaints reach 21% of reviews and cost an estimated 0.14★. Ingredients follow at 13% prevalence and 0.04★ — high for this category, and consistent with a shopper reading the label before the packet. Condition problems are rarer (6%) but carry the heaviest per-review penalty at 0.84★.
snack.language_argument: The praise vocabulary is diet-aware — “calories”, “low” — while the complaint side names specific attributes (“sea salt”, “oil”, “awful”). That asymmetry is a gift: people are telling you which formulation choice lost them, not merely that they were unhappy.

drink.headline: 436 reviews at 4.16★, and the most telling word in the whole category sits on the wrong side: “natural” is among the strongest markers of a *low*-rated drink review.
drink.fix_argument: Taste drives 0.15★ of drag at 24% prevalence. Ingredients are unusually prominent here — 17% of reviews complain about them, the second-highest of any category — for 0.06★. Together they say the same thing: this is a category where the label sets an expectation the liquid has to meet.
drink.language_argument: “Natural” appearing on the complaint side is the finding worth acting on. When a natural claim is the thing a reviewer reaches for while giving one star, the claim is being read as a promise about taste and then falling short. “Disappointed” and “smell” sit alongside it. Under-claim on naturalness; over-deliver on flavour.

baby & pet.headline: 431 reviews at 4.17★ and the highest complaint density in the dataset — 35% of sentences are negative. It is also the category where the analysis has to admit what it cannot rank.
baby & pet.fix_argument: Pet health effects and pet palatability together dominate the conversation — 413 mentions of health effects and 144 of palatability, the latter 53.5% negative — but neither shows a statistically reliable association with the star rating, so neither can be honestly placed on a ranked fix list. What can be ranked is taste (18% prevalence, 0.11★ drag) and ingredients (8%, 0.03★). The absence is itself informative: owners describe their animal's reaction at length, but that reaction does not translate cleanly into stars.
baby & pet.language_argument: The single strongest complaint marker in this category is “china”. Country of origin is doing real work in how pet owners judge a product, independently of the product itself. Praise runs on “loves”, “healthy”, “dog loves” — the animal's verdict, reported secondhand.

tea.headline: 334 reviews at 4.38★, the highest-rated substantial category — and the one that shows most clearly why a complaint is not always a problem.
tea.fix_argument: Taste complaints, at 26% prevalence, carry 0.16★ of drag and are the whole fix list of consequence. Ingredients and packaging together add 0.05★. But the more interesting number is a positive one: complaints about being unable to find a tea are associated with a rating 0.22★ *higher*, not lower. Scarcity complaints in tea come from devotees. Treat them as a distribution signal, not a defect.
tea.language_argument: Complaint terms are comparative — “taste like”, “compared”, “doesn't taste” — reviewers measuring a tea against one they already know. Praise is possessive: “favorite”, “enjoy”, “best”. In a category where people arrive with a reference point, naming the reference beats describing the flavour.

candy.headline: 285 reviews at 4.27★, with the highest taste-complaint prevalence of any category — 28% of reviews say the flavour was wrong.
candy.fix_argument: That taste prevalence produces 0.18★ of drag, the largest single-theme figure in the dataset outside condiments. Condition adds 0.05★ at 6% prevalence — in candy, arriving melted or stale is a real and separate failure. Ingredients contribute 0.03★.
candy.language_argument: “Artificial” is among the strongest complaint markers, sitting directly opposite “delicious” and “chocolate” on the praise side. “Money” also appears on the complaint side, which in a low-ticket category usually signals a portion or count disappointment rather than a price objection.

staples.headline: 256 reviews at 4.38★ — a category bought on specification rather than impulse, and the language shows it: “gluten free” and “organic” are among the strongest praise markers.
staples.fix_argument: Taste still leads at 22% prevalence and 0.14★, but ingredients are close behind at 16% prevalence for 0.05★ — the second-highest ingredient prevalence in the dataset. In a category where people buy to a dietary requirement, the ingredient list is the product.
staples.language_argument: Praise names categories and certifications — “pasta”, “gluten free”, “organic”. Complaints name containers — “box”, “cans”, “cup”, “flour”. Buyers here are specifying, and the failures are about what physically arrived versus what was specified.

other.headline: 249 uncategorised reviews at 3.90★ — the lowest-rated group, and the one where packaging fails most often: 48.9% of packaging mentions here are negative.
other.fix_argument: The fix list is unusually flat: taste 0.08★, condition 0.06★, packaging 0.02★. No single theme dominates, which is what a residual category should look like. Condition's 8% prevalence is the second-highest in the dataset — these are products that frequently arrive wrong.
other.language_argument: Complaint language is procedural — “can't”, “item”, “purchase”, “brand” — rather than sensory. People in this bucket are describing transactions that failed, not products they disliked. Read this category as a fulfilment signal more than a product one.

condiments.headline: 236 reviews at 4.13★, carrying the largest taste drag in the dataset: 31% of reviews complain about flavour, for an estimated 0.20★.
condiments.fix_argument: Taste at 0.20★ and ingredients at 0.07★ — the highest ingredient prevalence anywhere, 22% — make this the category where the recipe itself is most often the problem. Price adds 0.03★. Together they describe a category bought for a specific culinary effect, where missing that effect is unforgiving.
condiments.language_argument: “Artificial” and “tasted” lead the complaints; “coconut oil”, “hot” and “tasting” lead the praise. Reviewers name the ingredient they wanted and the aftertaste they got. Specificity in the listing — what it tastes of, what it is made from — is the whole marketing job here.

protein snacks.headline: 137 reviews at 3.88★ — the lowest-rated category in the dataset, and the only one where how the product *arrived* is a top-two problem.
protein snacks.fix_argument: Condition and expectations reach 14% prevalence here — the highest of any category that clears the 15-review floor for ranking — producing 0.12★ of drag on top of taste's 0.17★. Of the 26 condition mentions, 84.6% are negative. The complaint vocabulary names the mechanism directly: “description”, “date”, “bag”. These are products arriving close to or past their date, in packaging that failed.
protein snacks.language_argument: “Texture” and “disappointed” round out the complaints — in protein bars and jerky, texture failure is what staleness feels like to the eater. Fixing date rotation and seal integrity would likely move more stars here than any recipe change.

seasoning & spice.headline: 112 reviews at 4.37★. Well-liked, and thin enough that only the two largest effects can be stated with confidence.
seasoning & spice.fix_argument: Taste complaints at 27% prevalence produce 0.17★ of drag; ingredients at 20% produce 0.07★. Both are high-prevalence for a category with a high mean rating, which suggests a product people mostly love and occasionally find mis-blended.
seasoning & spice.language_argument: No distinguishing-language analysis is reported: with only 13 low-rated reviews, weighted log-odds would be estimating vocabulary differences from a sample too small to be meaningful. Reporting a phrase list here would be inventing precision.

chocolate.headline: 103 reviews at 4.29★, and exactly one theme clears the bar for a ranked recommendation.
chocolate.fix_argument: Taste complaints appear in 28% of reviews and carry 0.18★ of drag. Nothing else in the category reaches both the 15-review floor and statistical significance — with 103 reviews, that is the honest ceiling on what can be claimed. Texture is 32% negative across 50 mentions and is worth watching as the sample grows.
chocolate.language_argument: Not reported — 13 low-rated reviews is too thin a base for a vocabulary comparison.

baked goods.headline: 91 reviews at 4.28★. The smallest category that still supports a ranked finding, and only just.
baked goods.fix_argument: Taste complaints at 23% prevalence produce 0.15★ of drag. That is the only effect here that survives both the sample-size floor and significance testing. Texture, at 30% negative across 50 mentions, is the obvious second candidate and cannot yet be separated from noise.
baked goods.language_argument: Not reported — only 13 low-rated reviews, below the threshold for a stable comparison.

dairy.headline: 74 reviews at 4.06★ — the only category in the dataset where taste is not the leading fixable problem.
dairy.fix_argument: Ingredients are the single ranked theme, at 20% prevalence for 0.07★ of drag. Taste generates 81 mentions here and is only 21% negative — behind snack, coffee and tea, and below every other category in the dataset. Dairy buyers appear to like how these products taste and to object to what is in them.
dairy.language_argument: Not reported — 14 low-rated reviews is too small a base. With a larger sample this is the category whose vocabulary would be most worth revisiting, since the ingredient-over-taste pattern is unusual enough to want confirming.
